note: No source found gives a year, century or millennium for the start of Auquilohuagra; Wikipedia calls it only an archaeological site and the inventory says pre-Inca.

Wikipedia says only 'first stage of development' of the Chimu culture; the only readable-to-me dated claims (a Chimu-period range, a XIV century claim on a page that refuses plain requests) are not a verifiable date for the building's start.
The Wikipedia articles only say the pyramid was built in the Fourth Dynasty; no readable source dates this pyramid's construction to a year or century, so it stays empty.

No quotable source gives the site's own point in the required form. The English article has an empty coordinates field and the Wikidata item carries no P625; the national register record gives no georeferencing, and its open-data listing prints longitude before latitude, which the field's format rule does not accept. The OpenStreetMap link near the article name resolves to an unrelated node in California, so it is not evidence for this site.

No source dates the start of Wamanmarka. The national heritage register record describes a pre-Inca citadel with influences of the Collao and Wari cultures and evidence of the Inca culture, and gives only the 2011 heritage declaration, but no year, century or millennium - and period words alone do not date a site.
The sources found give only period words (Inca Late Horizon, earlier Wari presence) or speculation, no year or century for the start of the site.

The English Wikipedia article on the Huilai site gives no date at all, and the Chinese article dates it only relatively: '涵蓋將近四千年的時間範圍' (spans nearly four thousand years) and the earliest layer is said to reach back to the Neolithic. Neither is a year, century or millennium, so no source dates the start.

Sources date only the murals (Xolalpan phase c. 450-650 AD on Wikipedia; roughly 350-650 CE on Yucatan Magazine) or Teotihuacan as a whole; none gives the construction or first occupation of the Atetelco compound itself, and a mural date is not the start of the site.

The English Wikipedia article describes Yuraq Mach'ay only as an archaeological site with rock paintings at 3,991 m on the slope of Pukara, and gives no year, century or millennium for its start; a Quechua name gloss ('white cave') is not a date.
No source dates the start of Tarmatambo; the English article gives only its National Cultural Heritage designation, and the Spanish one calls it an ancient Inca llacta without a year.

The only source, the Megalithic Portal entry, says its location is approximate and actually cites the peak of the Paricutin volcano which towers over the dig site, so it is not the site's own point and no other source gives one.
The entry covers the megaliths of a whole German state; no source gives a single point for it, and the English article prints no coordinates.

The Somerset HER and Wikipedia give only 'Early Iron Age' or the generic hill-fort statement ('roughly the start of the first millennium BC' for hill forts in general); no source dates this fort's start.

English and Spanish Wikipedia and Wikidata print no point for La Joyanca, and none of the excavation or project pages (CEMCA, CNRS ArchAm, openedition, Cambridge) shows one in plain text; the only point found, Mapcarta's 17.23769, -90.56879, is an OpenStreetMap aggregator point 25 km from the stored one near El Peru-Waka' and cannot be reconciled, so no quotable source exists.
No readable source gives a point for Tampu Mach'ay in Acostambo, Huancavelica; Wikipedia and Wikidata carry none, and the linked pages are about Tambomachay near Cusco.
No source dates Tampu Mach'ay in Huancavelica.
No source prints a point for this site: the discoverer withheld the precise location for fear of looting, and the Megalithic Portal entry itself notes its point is for a nearby village, not the site.
Wikipedia marks the coordinates as missing and Wikidata has no P625; no readable source found gives a point for Llaqta Qulluy in Conayca.
No readable source dates Llaqta Qulluy in Conayca; Wikipedia only gives the name's meaning.

Wikipedia says only that the site existed before the Roman era and was abandoned perhaps shortly after 360; the Princeton Encyclopedia and Herefordshire HER give finds (coins from Claudius, a peak in the 3rd and early 4th c.) but no year, century or millennium for the foundation or start of the site.

A SciELO article prints 18 37 40 N y 97 42 59 W for the site, but the connecting word makes the quote unreadable as a point; the INAH pages only hold the point in map scripts, not visible text. No quotable point found.

The Cultural Inventory record for the Ayşepınar rock tombs, which is the only register page I could read, prints no coordinates in its visible text, and I found no other readable source that quotes a point for the site. The stored point stays and the site goes to the owner's list.

The Cultural Inventory dates the Ayşepınar rock tombs only to the Hellenistic-Roman period, a period word, and mentions objects of the 5000s BC as stray finds from the area without dating the site itself. A period word does not date the start, so the empty field stays empty.

No readable page dates the construction of the Devil's Causeway to a year, century or millennium: English Wikipedia only says the road is 'thought to pre-date Hadrian's Wall' and the North East Research Framework speaks of a 'Flavian or Trajanic' fort on its route, i.e. period words without a year. The Bernician Studies Group review that dates the road to the mid-first to early second century is a PDF, which the quote check cannot read.

The English Wikipedia article prints no coordinate for Waraqu Urqu itself; its only point, 13°07'13"S 73°49'57"W, is explicitly given for the nearby mountain Wanaku Urqu (guanaco mountain), which the brief excludes as a namesake, not the site. No readable source prints a point for the site itself, so the stored point stays and the site goes to the owner's list.

No source I could read dates the start of Waraqu Urqu: the article names only the Chanka culture as its period, a period word that does not date a start, and the linked 2025 news about a 3,000-year-old city concerns a different site in Puno.

The English and Spanish Wikipedia articles on Montana (Escuintla, Guatemala) print no coordinates and the Wikidata item has no P625; no other reputable page was found that prints a point for the site.
No source found dates Awkimarka/Auquimarca in Tomay Kichwa District, Ambo Province, Huánuco; Wikipedia gives no date and the press and tourism pages found name only 'pre-Inca'.
